data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Scientific theories aim at universal truth, shields only at immediate survival","Corroboration involves logical falsification attempts, not just physical impact","Theory choice affects the definition of reality, unlike shield choice"],"overturn_conditions":["If the goal of science is shown to be something other than verisimilitude (e.g., empirical adequacy only)","If past performance is demonstrated to be logically irrelevant to any form of rational choice"],"shared_structure":["Selection based on past performance under stress","No guarantee of future success","Rationality defined by adherence to protocol rather than prediction accuracy","Goal-oriented behavior despite uncertainty"],"source_memory_refs":["shield_battle_test","medical_triage_protocol"],"transfer_claims":["Just as a commander rationally chooses the battle-tested shield without believing it is invincible, a scientist rationally chooses the well-corroborated theory without believing it is probable.","The rationality of the choice lies in the procedure (testing/critical scrutiny), not in the outcome prediction."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of truth, but as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in the aim of science (verisimilitude) and the pragmatic necessity of action, without smuggling in probability; however, accepting this defense costs the ability to claim that corroboration provides any rational degree of belief in the theory's future success, reducing the preference to a bold guess with no epistemic weight beyond its survival of past tests.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude is formally incoherent (as Miller and Tich\u00fd argued), then the aim of science cannot rationally guide theory choice, collapsing the defense into mere convention.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for corroborated theories implies any expectation of future success based on past performance, it constitutes induction by another name, violating Popper's core prohibition.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'pragmatic necessity' argument fails to distinguish between acting on a hunch and acting on a rational rule, the preference becomes arbitrary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'logical probability' (which Popper rejects as increasing with corroboration) and 'methodological choice' (which is governed by the goal of approaching truth). It posits that preferring the best-tested theory is analogous to choosing the strongest shield in battle: one does not believe the shield is magically impenetrable (induction), but one chooses it because it has withstood the hardest blows (corroboration) while acknowledging it might fail next time. This separates the justification for action from the justification for belief.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
